The velocity of sound in seawater varies from about 1450 m/s to 1550 m/s, increasing with temperature, salinity, and pressure.
Sound channels, such as the mixed-layer sound channel and the deep sound (SOFAR) channel, can trap sound waves and enable efficient long-range propagation.

The Thorp equation describes the frequency-dependent absorption coefficient of low-frequency sound (0.1-20 kHz) in the ocean, accounting for boric acid/borate, magnesium sulfate, and high-frequency relaxation processes.

Diffraction can significantly contribute to attenuation below 0.2 kHz in shallow water, while diffusive scattering can affect frequencies below 0.5 kHz in shallow water and 0.2 kHz in deep ocean channels.

Laboratory studies have shown that the boric acid-borate equilibrium in seawater is responsible for a relaxation process that contributes to the anomalous absorption of low-frequency sound (below 1 kHz) observed in deep ocean channels.

The boric acid-mediated sound absorption is relatively small, on the order of 0.05 dB/km at 500 Hz, but can be significantly greater than the contributions from other physical processes at these frequencies.

The exact form of the frequency dependence of the absorption coefficient can vary from ocean to ocean and from water mass to water mass, likely due to differences in the chemical composition and speciation of the water.
The boric acid-borate equilibrium is coupled with other equilibria in seawater, such as those involving magnesium and carbonate, which may also influence the overall sound absorption.

The interpretation of the experimental data on low-frequency sound attenuation in the ocean is complicated by the contributions of various physical processes and the need to separate the effects of chemical relaxation from other factors.

The paper suggests that much laboratory work still needs to be done to fully understand the interactions between boric acid and other ionic species in seawater and how these interactions influence the overall sound absorption.
Boron in seawater occurs primarily as inorganic borate, with only 1-3% of the total boron associated as organically bound boron.
The pKa of boric acid in seawater ranges from 8.86 (5°C) to 8.61 (25°C) at 36% salinity and atmospheric pressure.
The boric acid-borate relaxation process is accompanied by a large increase in volume (ΔV° = 36 cc/mol).
Dilution of seawater with NaCl solution and subsequent addition of borax can shift the relaxation resonance frequency, confirming the role of boron in the low-frequency sound absorption.

Correlations have been found between the acoustical amplitude parameter (cλ)max and the pH of the water mass, as well as between the relaxation frequency and the salinity (and hence total boron concentration) of the medium.
